source.title: Improving Performance in Neural Networks by Dendrites-Activated Connections
source.authors: C. Metta; Marco Fantozzi; Andrea Papini; G. Amato; Matteo Bergamaschi; S. Galfrè; A. Marchetti; Michelangelo Vegliò; M. Parton; F. Morandin

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper sweeps neural-network sizes and reports test error, so its results bear on the model-size/test-error part of V1. It does not measure interpolation or test for the fall-rise-fall curve itself.
record.gate_note: The SGEMM experiments vary network width and parameter count and report test MSE. They do not measure training-set fit or identify an interpolation threshold. The paper's experiments about DAC versus baseline accuracy are not, by themselves, evidence for the double-descent shape.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a new unit (DAC, unshared pre-activation biases) and compares it with baseline networks. It never mentions or cites double descent. It does not measure training fit or an interpolation threshold. Its SGEMM width sweep uses early stopping and L2 regularization, which keeps training away from the interpolating regime. No result bears on any version. 'cites_only' is the closest enum value; strictly, the paper neither cites nor uses the claim (T6).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that pre-activation with unshared biases (DAC) improves accuracy across architectures and datasets. They also conclude that, for SGEMM networks where adding width stops helping, adding biases is more efficient than adding weights. They say nothing about double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares standard networks with a proposed DAC architecture; it does not use the original double-descent method or measure interpolation thresholds.
record.method_sensitivity: For SGEMM, the reported benefit of DAC depends on network size: DAC performs similarly or worse for smaller networks and better for larger ones. The paper also reports weak dependence on depth for the task.
record.problems: The relevant size results do not report training-set fit or locate the interpolation threshold. The SGEMM size comparisons are reported mainly in plots; exact point values are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports test-error results for VGG and ResNet architectures at different depths and datasets (Figures 5–6 and Tables 1–2), plus ISIC results. These are DAC-versus-baseline performance comparisons, not measurements locating or testing the double-descent peak; they were left out for that reason.

untested.parts: All of it: no interpolation threshold, no peak, no second descent measured. Training used early stopping, which precludes the regime.
All of it: epoch-wise test-error curves are not reported; only best-epoch errors are given.
All of it: training-set size is not varied.
All of it: no label-noise or regularization sweep.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's relation 'tests'/T2 is wrong. A size sweep with early stopping and no training-fit measurement cannot bear on V1. The DAC-vs-baseline rows are method comparisons. The paper never mentions double descent; it was likely retrieved by keyword (parameters vs. performance).

versions.untested_parts: The size sweep does not locate the just-fits-training-set point or test whether test error peaks there and descends afterward; the reported evidence is limited to the tested sizes and task.

rows.subject: SGEMM rectangular baseline networks (aggregated over depths)
rows.size_stated: Widths 17, 25, 35, 50, 70, 100, 141 and 200 are shown in the parameter-doubling analysis; the size range across architectures was 1700 to 1.4M trainable parameters.
rows.operation_detail: Compared test MSE as the number of parameters increased by increasing width.

conditions.value: averaged across depths; depths showed no dependence in the reported comparison

rows.measure: Test MSE variation (log-MSE variation in nats)
rows.value: Increasing weights gives large benefits for small sizes and almost no improvement from 141 to 200 units per layer.
rows.uncertainty: Sample standard deviation shown as error bars; exact values not stated in text.
rows.locator: Section 5, SGEMM performance regression; Figure 4 and Appendix Figure 9
rows.note: The text describes diminishing returns from increasing width, but does not report training fit or place any point relative to an interpolation threshold.
rows.check: The baseline width sweep (Fig. 4) is a parameter-doubling efficiency analysis under early stopping, with no training error and no interpolation point. It cannot show a peak or a second descent. The reported trend is diminishing returns with width, which is not a V1 test.

rows.subject: SGEMM rectangular networks with DAC (aggregated over depths)
rows.size_stated: DAC models were constructed to have almost the same total trainable parameters as their paired baselines; the parameter range across architectures was 1700 to 1.4M.
rows.operation_detail: Compared test MSE after replacing shared biases with unshared biases, approximately doubling parameters in the parameter-doubling analysis.

conditions.value: averaged across depths; depths showed no dependence in the reported comparison

rows.measure: Test MSE variation (log-MSE variation in nats)
rows.value: Making biases unshared gives a uniform improvement of about 0.25 nats in test error.
rows.uncertainty: Sample standard deviation shown as error bars; exact values not stated in text.
rows.note: This reports the effect of a parameter increase through unshared biases, not a double-descent curve or a peak near interpolation.
rows.check: This row compares the study's own method (unshared biases) with adding weights. It should not be a row for the double-descent claim.

rows.subject: SGEMM fully connected networks (baseline and DAC, aggregate)
rows.size_stated: The paper reports sizes from 1700 to 1.4M trainable parameters; Appendix Figure 8 plots results across parameter counts.
rows.operation_detail: Compared test MSE across network sizes and shapes.
rows.value: The paper states that DAC networks perform worse up to 10^4 parameters, but generally better above 10^5 parameters, also exceeding the best baseline results.
rows.note: The report describes relative performance over parameter ranges but does not establish whether either curve rises to a peak near an interpolation threshold.
rows.check: This row compares DAC with the baseline across parameter counts (Fig. 8). It is the study's own method against a comparator, not a measure of the test-error curve shape relative to interpolation. It should not be a row.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
